passage: Mentoring note, Ira. Sonali came to our monthly one-to-one with a single page: two projects, the churn dashboard and the onboarding revamp, both tied to the team's target for the year. When I asked why not the three others on her plate, she explained aloud that these two were what the promotion criteria measure: results the team can point to. Halfway through, a colleague messaged her for help with a slide deck. Sonali replied politely, "Not this month, but here's a template that might help." She glanced at me and shrugged. What I did next: I moved one small recurring task of hers to another team and asked her to bring me anything unclear about priorities. Three months later both projects had numbers beside them.

qa.q: Which two projects did Sonali choose?
qa.a: Sonali chose the churn dashboard and the onboarding revamp.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling when she declined the colleague's request?
qa.a: Sonali was probably a little uneasy about saying no but stayed firm and polite, glancing at Ira and shrugging.

qa.q: What else could Sonali do to keep her focus, and why?
qa.a: Sonali could keep a short list of what she has declined and why, because it helps her explain her priorities to her manager.

qa.q: How might the colleague who asked for help have seen the polite refusal?
qa.a: The colleague may feel a bit disappointed, but the template offered in reply shows that Sonali still cares about helping.

grounding: Illustrates picking two projects tied to team targets, politely declining smaller requests and delivering clear results that match promotion criteria.

Sunday, 11 p.m.

Wrote down everything I said yes to this quarter. Nineteen things. Nineteen! Newsletter, intern buddy, two lunch-and-learns, the office move spreadsheet...
Then I put the team lead criteria next to it. The ones that count: moving the team's onboarding target, and owning a project end to end. Which of my nineteen touch those? Two. The onboarding redesign and the partner portal.
So here's the thinking. If I spread thin, I finish nothing well. If I pick those two and do them properly, I'll have real results to show.
Tomorrow I'm telling Naveen I'll hand back the newsletter and the lunch-and-learns. Politely. "I'd love to, but I'm focusing on onboarding this quarter." Practised it twice already.
Scary. Also a relief.
— Vasudha

qa.q: How many things had Vasudha said yes to this quarter?
How does Vasudha feel about saying no to Naveen?
qa.a: Vasudha feels scared about turning down requests but also relieved, because focusing on two projects makes the goal feel reachable.

qa.q: What else could Vasudha do to check the choice of the two projects?
qa.a: Vasudha could ask Naveen whether the onboarding redesign and partner portal are the results the criteria reward, so the focus is confirmed before declining the rest.

qa.q: How might Naveen see Vasudha handing back the newsletter?
qa.a: Naveen may be a little disappointed to lose the help, but a polite, clear reason about onboarding makes the choice easy to respect.

grounding: It shows someone choosing two projects tied to team targets and politely declining smaller requests so they can deliver clear results that match the criteria.
